newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai currency woes delay rate cuts, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Thai currency woes delay rate cuts, analysts say.

text.p: Pressure on the battered baht has left the Bank of Thailand few options but to delay plans to ease high Thai interest rates in order to stimulate the sluggish national economy, analysts said.
The heady surge of the dollar has triggered a flight from the baht, wreaked havoc on rates in the Thai money market, and prolonged a severe slump on the stock market.

The baht has found itself a target of renewed attacks by offshore speculators spurred by rumours that Thailand later this year may choose to devalue its currency, which is pegged to a basket of currencies but heavily weighted to the dollar.
Analysts had expected the current 13.5 percent average Thai prime lending rate to ease by up to two percent this year.
But Somchai Trairattanapirom, head of research at SITCA Investment and Securities Plc, said the run on the baht would delay the rate cuts until at least late in the second quarter.
"The current environment makes it very difficult to match various maturing funds, and I don't see interest rates coming down before late in the second quarter," he said.
But Jan Cherim, general manager of ING Bank, was among bankers who expected the central bank to prove currency speculators wrong.

"The current round of baht panic has not been supported by fundamentals. I regard baht pressure as foreign exchange market nonsense," he said. "Suddenly the profile of baht has come up in the minds of currency dealers."

The devaluation talk in the past few weeks hastened a flight from baht-denominated stocks and deposits to assets held in dollars. The switch dried up money market liquidity, pushing the overnight interbank rate to a new six-month high of 25 percent.

Cherim said the baht had also depreciated against the dollar despite their partial tie, and he saw no political reasons for Thailand to devalue the currency as it would sharply raise import financing and aggravate its troubled property sector.

Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan and central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond issued almost daily reassurances last week that they saw no reason to devalue the baht despite its recent gains against the yen and mark.

They warned that Thai short-term interest rates may remain high and a liquidity crunch would put a squeeze on speculators by raising the cost of shifting baht funds to dollars and also induce fund managers to maintain high-yield baht deposits.
Thailand gave baht stability a higher priority than its earlier plan to engineer lower rates to help boost the economy, which grew 6.7 percent in 1996, the slowest in 10 years.
Krungthai Thanakit Plc said in a report: "We continue to believe that a devaluation this year is less than probable, although it is clearly possible.
"Our view is that the baht will be able to sustain the pressure for the coming few weeks or months, after which those pressures should ease.
"With that easing, it will also be possible for the BoT to move towards easing the pressure on the real economy by engineering further reductions in short-term baht interest rates."
